consequence.explanation: The reported placebo median (1767 EUR) exceeds the reported Cerebrolysin median (1466 EUR), reversing the direction of the paper's central cost comparison -- that Cerebrolysin costs 408 EUR more per patient than standard care -- which is the numerator of every ICER reported.

findings.notes: This is the strongest finding in the paper. A median of 1767 requires at least half the sample to sit at or above 1767, i.e. at or above 7.10 standard deviations above the reported mean of 1050. Cantelli's inequality caps the achievable share at 0.0195, so no distribution whatsoever -- not merely no normal one -- can carry mean 1050, SD 101 and median 1767 simultaneously; the tool reports distribution_free_violation = true, so the verdict does NOT rest on a normality assumption about skewed cost data. Inputs were re-read from the get_table grid before flagging. The remaining Table 1 statistics are mutually coherent (see cerebrolysin_median_consistent, ci_consistency_both_arms), which isolates this single cell: SD 101 with n = 93 reproduces the printed 95% bounds almost exactly, so the mean, SD and interval agree and only the median dissents. The most economical explanation is a transcription error (e.g. 1067 mis-set as 1767), but as printed the row is not internally satisfiable. I have recorded the tool's own severity of highly_suspicious rather than escalating to impossible: the Cantelli contradiction is exact arithmetic, and the editorial stage may reasonably treat it as such. The supplementary Cost worksheet contains the per-patient costs that would settle this immediately.

findings.notes: Recorded at suspicious although the tool returned highly_suspicious, and the reason is specific. The aggregate count is inflated by two classes of legitimate repetition that rulebook rule 11 requires me to discount first: (a) design constants -- the value 207.9 recurs 93 times in a single contiguous run in Cost column K, and 93 is exactly the placebo arm size, so this is an arm-level constant I should have passed in exclude_columns; and (b) finite-lookup ties -- SF-6D utilities come from a discrete converter, so single values recur heavily by construction (0.6166 appears 27 times in one column, 0.6228 and 0.7476 four times each). What those guards do NOT explain is the row-pair signal, which I verified directly against the raw grid rather than trusting the aggregate: patients P-2-29 and P-2-32, two distinct placebo IDs, carry identical values in all nine numeric columns -- six independent utility lookups at two separate visits plus three derived QALYs agreeing to 17 significant figures. That is possible innocently only if both patients returned the same SF-6D health state at BOTH visit 2 and visit 7. 75 such pairs were flagged and row-pair coverage is PARTIAL, so 75 is a floor, not a count. Adjudicating this needs the underlying SF-36 item responses, which are not in the workbook. Only one pair was individually verified; the other 74 are asserted by the tool and unexamined.
